questions.stem: What is Data Leakage in Machine Learning, and why can it make a model appear more accurate during testing than it will be in real-world use?
options: Data leakage occurs when strongly predictive features are included during training, even when those features are available before every real prediction. This makes evaluation scores unreliable.
Data Leakage occurs when a model uses information that should not be available during training or prediction. This can produce artificially high evaluation scores and poor performance on new data.
Data leakage occurs when a model is evaluated on unfamiliar test records after training, because using any held-out data to measure performance introduces forbidden information.
Data leakage occurs when duplicate examples cross dataset splits, but using future events to build training features remains acceptable if the records themselves are different.

questions.stem: What are Target Leakage and Train-Test Contamination, and how do these two types of Data Leakage differ?
options: Target Leakage occurs when a test label guides preprocessing, while Train-Test Contamination occurs when a feature reveals an outcome that will not exist at prediction time.
Target Leakage occurs when a feature is highly predictive, even if it is available before the decision. Train-Test Contamination requires directly copying test labels into training.

Target Leakage occurs when future target details appear in features, while Train-Test Contamination happens only when identical rows appear in both sets, not when test statistics influence preprocessing.

Target Leakage occurs when a feature reveals target information unavailable at prediction time. Train-Test Contamination occurs when information from test data influences model training or preprocessing.

questions.stem: Why must preprocessing methods such as scaling, missing-value imputation, and feature selection be fitted only on training data rather than the entire dataset?
options: Fitting preprocessing methods on the entire dataset allows test information to influence the model. Fitting them only on training data keeps test data independent and produces more reliable evaluation results.
Preprocessing should use the full dataset before splitting when it does not read target labels, because estimating scaling or imputation statistics from test inputs cannot affect evaluation.
Preprocessing should be fitted separately on training and test data so each group receives its own scaling, missing-value replacements, and selected features during the final evaluation.
Preprocessing can be fitted on all available rows after the train-test split as long as the estimator is trained only on training labels and the test labels remain hidden.

questions.stem: How can Data Leakage occur during cross-validation when preprocessing, feature selection, or data augmentation is performed before creating validation folds?
options: Cross-validation prevents leakage once folds are created, so fitting a scaler or feature selector on the entire dataset beforehand is safe if the target labels were not used.
Data augmentation can occur before creating validation folds when the transformed examples retain their original labels, because those new examples count as independent observations.

Leakage occurs when preprocessing or feature selection uses validation data, or when related augmented samples appear in both training and validation folds. These operations must respect training and validation boundaries.
Feature engineering can use every validation fold to identify useful features, provided the final model is fitted only on its training fold and scored on held-out labels.

questions.stem: How do Scikit-learn Pipelines and proper train-test splitting help prevent Data Leakage during Machine Learning model development?
options: Scikit-learn Pipelines prevent leakage by learning common scaling and feature-selection settings from all available records first, then running the classifier on each separate training split.
Scikit-learn Pipelines fit preprocessing and model steps using only training data within each split. Proper train-test splitting prevents evaluation data from influencing the training process.
Proper splitting makes independent preprocessing unnecessary because separately applying feature selection to the held-out test data preserves the same features without exposing its labels.
A Pipeline automatically protects the final test set even when feature selection and missing-value imputation were already fitted outside the Pipeline using all available data.

questions.stem: Why can random train-test splitting cause Data Leakage in time-series datasets or datasets containing repeated observations from the same users, patients, or devices?
options: Random splitting is reliable for time series when class proportions stay similar across sets, because balanced labels prevent future information from leaking into earlier records.
Random splitting is appropriate for repeated measurements if each record has a different timestamp, even when the same person or device appears in both evaluation and training.
Time-based splitting solves leakage for every grouped dataset, so observations from the same user may safely appear on both sides if their timestamps are ordered correctly.

Random splitting can expose future information or place related observations in both training and testing sets. Time-based and group-aware splitting help prevent leakage by keeping future or related data separated.

questions.stem: How can Data Leakage be detected and prevented in production Machine Learning systems using point-in-time validation, feature availability checks, and data lineage?
options: Point-in-time validation verifies that features use only information available at prediction time. Feature availability checks and data lineage help detect future information, hidden target details, and contamination between datasets.
Point-in-time validation checks feature timestamps against the model training date rather than each prediction date; this makes future information safe when it came from trusted sources.
Production leakage checks can rely on data lineage alone because knowing the source of a feature proves it was available at prediction time and independent of the target.
Feature availability can be confirmed using the date a dataset was downloaded, while point-in-time tests may combine later events if the historical labels are hidden.
